newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian truckers stage nationwide strike.
newsitem.headline: Colombian truckers stage nationwide strike.

text.p: Truck drivers began a nationwide work stoppage early on Monday, prompting the government to warn of stiff penalties if they tried to put a stranglehold on the economy by shutting down Colombia's leading highways.

The strike by the Colombian Truck Drivers Association began at midnight on Sunday and union spokesmen said it would continue until the government ceded to demands that include calls for higher tariffs, lower taxes and tolls and tighter security on the country's roadways.
"It would be very serious to blockade roadways in a bid to paralyse the country. This is something the government cannot allow," Transportation Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez Gutierrez said.

Speaking in an interview with the RCN radio network, he warned that any trucking company whose drivers were caught blockading roadways would face the revocation of their operating licenses, among other sanctions.
Individual drivers would also be punished with the loss of their trucker's licenses and the cancellation of vehicle permits, Lopez said.
Truckers were among the hardest hit by a nationwide leftist guerrilla offensive beginning in late August. Scores of commercial vehicles were firebombed.

The Drivers Association is also calling for the lifting of a recent ban on the use of vehicles that are more than 16 years old for overland cargo hauling, a regulation that could put thousands of independent operators out of business.
Monday was a national holiday in Colombia, making it difficult for authorities to gauge the effects of the strike on its first day.
But Luz Mari Tangarife, executive secretary of the Drivers Association, said about 100,000 trucks that might otherwise have been working had stayed off the nation's roadways.
There were no immediate reports of violence stemming from the strike and Tangarife said there were also no immediate plans to block highways to draw attention to the stoppage.

Among other effects that will become evident as the job action takes hold later this week, she said it would undoubtedly delay shipments of coffee and coal to Colombia's ports. Coffee is particularly sensitive since the largest harvest of the year is already in full swing.
